lessons.pitfall: Resetting a processor does not necessarily reset every peripheral or erase retained state; inspect domain behavior.
lessons.exercise: Describe one test for a power failure during a firmware update.
lessons.solution: Interrupt the update at several write boundaries, reboot, and verify that either the previous valid image or a fully verified new image runs, with a defined recovery path when neither is valid.

quiz.question: A 256-byte window starts at 0x1000. Its final byte is:
quiz.explanation: The end is base+size−1.

modules.title: Embedded Linux, networks, and security
modules.summary: Connect devices to operating systems and reliable remote interfaces.

lessons.title: Processes, drivers, and device descriptions
lessons.explanation: An operating system isolates processes and mediates access to hardware. A driver translates OS-facing operations into device-specific behavior. A device tree describes hardware topology and resources for platforms that use it; it is not executable driver code. Build configuration, kernel version, bootloader, root filesystem, and hardware description must agree. Start debugging from boot logs and the simplest observable interface.
lessons.relationship: User process → system call → kernel subsystem → driver → peripheral
lessons.example: A serial device can fail because its driver is absent, its clock is wrong, its pin mux is wrong, or its device description names the wrong address. Recompiling the application alone cannot fix these underlying integration errors.
lessons.pitfall: A node in a device tree does not manufacture missing hardware or guarantee that a compatible driver is enabled.
lessons.exercise: Name evidence that distinguishes an application permission problem from a peripheral failing to probe.
lessons.solution: Check whether the device exists and whether kernel logs show a successful probe, then inspect access permissions and the application’s actual error.

lessons.title: Packets, framing, and resilient protocols
lessons.explanation: A byte stream does not preserve application-message boundaries. Define framing, lengths, versioning, checksums, and timeouts explicitly. Network protocols differ in reliability and ordering guarantees, but applications still need limits and recovery behavior. Parse untrusted input defensively and reject oversized or malformed frames before allocating large buffers or changing state. A protocol should remain understandable after a dropped byte or interrupted connection.
lessons.relationship: A frame can use version + payload length + payload + integrity field
lessons.example: For a two-byte big-endian payload length, bytes 0x01 0x00 describe 256 bytes. A parser receiving only 100 bytes must wait or timeout; it must not treat missing bytes as valid data. Set an application maximum even if the field can encode more.
lessons.pitfall: A TCP read returning 20 bytes does not prove that one complete 20-byte application message has arrived.
lessons.exercise: A frame declares 2000 bytes but your maximum is 512. What should the parser do before allocating payload storage?
lessons.solution: Reject the frame or close/reset the parser according to the protocol. Do not trust the length merely because it fits the field width.

lessons.title: Threat models and update design
lessons.explanation: Security begins by identifying assets, attackers, trust boundaries, and plausible failure consequences. Debug ports, stored credentials, network parsers, and update mechanisms each expose different attack surfaces. Cryptographic verification requires correct key management and implementation; designing a novel cipher is not a useful shortcut. Treat fault recovery and secure updating as normal operating requirements, including interrupted writes and version rollback rules.
lessons.relationship: Authenticity answers who authorized data; integrity answers whether data changed
lessons.example: A CRC can detect many accidental transmission errors but an attacker can recompute it. A signature can authenticate an update under a trusted public key, while a version policy may be needed to reject an older but validly signed vulnerable image.
lessons.pitfall: Encryption alone does not imply authenticity, and a signed image alone does not establish a complete secure lifecycle.
lessons.exercise: Why might a device reject a correctly signed firmware image with a lower version number?
lessons.solution: A rollback policy can prevent reinstallation of known-vulnerable older software. The version state and recovery process also need protection.

quiz.question: A single TCP read always returns a complete application message.
quiz.explanation: A stream does not preserve application framing.

modules.title: PCB, power, and product reliability
modules.summary: Turn a schematic into a measurable, maintainable physical system.

lessons.title: Schematic capture and PCB return paths
lessons.explanation: A schematic records intended connectivity; a PCB implements that connectivity in a physical field environment. Placement, return-current paths, decoupling, connector pinouts, and assembly access influence behavior. Use electrical-rule checking and design-rule checking, then inspect assumptions the tools cannot know. Label test points and keep a bring-up plan so a manufactured board can be diagnosed rather than merely powered and hoped to work.
lessons.relationship: Loop inductance and return-path discontinuities can create noise even when net connectivity is correct
lessons.example: A high-frequency signal routed across a split reference plane forces return current around the gap, increasing loop area. Keeping an appropriate continuous return reference and locating decoupling close to supply pins can reduce unwanted impedance.
lessons.pitfall: “Ground” is not a perfect equipotential surface at all frequencies. A correct net name does not guarantee a good return path.
lessons.exercise: List three checks before powering a newly assembled low-voltage board.
lessons.solution: Inspect polarity and assembly, measure for shorts with power removed, and review a current-limited power-up sequence with expected rail values and accessible test points.

lessons.title: Power conversion and thermal budgets
lessons.explanation: Linear regulators dissipate the voltage difference as heat; switching converters trade additional circuit complexity and switching noise for potentially higher efficiency. Choose a regulator using load transients, dropout, stability requirements, layout, and thermal conditions, not only nominal current. Thermal resistance is a simplified steady-state model whose value depends strongly on the board and environment. Measure temperature after a controlled stabilization period.
lessons.relationship: PLDO=(Vin−Vout)I; approximate ΔT=P θJA under the specified thermal conditions
lessons.example: Dropping 5 V to 3.3 V at 0.2 A dissipates 0.34 W. If effective θJA is 100 °C/W, the estimated rise is 34 °C. At 40 °C ambient, the simplified junction estimate is 74 °C, before other heat sources and model uncertainty.
lessons.pitfall: A package’s headline current rating is not a guarantee that it can dissipate the required power on your board.
lessons.exercise: Estimate LDO dissipation for 12 V to 5 V at 0.1 A and temperature rise at 80 °C/W.
lessons.solution: Power is 0.7 W and estimated rise is 56 °C. This can motivate a different supply architecture.

lessons.title: Reliability, EMC, and test strategy
lessons.explanation: Reliability work asks how the product behaves across variation, aging, misuse, and failures. Define environmental limits and observable acceptance tests. EMI emission and susceptibility arise from current loops, coupling paths, and bandwidth; fixing them late can require board changes. Design-for-test adds access and diagnostics during development. A structured failure analysis prioritizes credible causes and mitigations without pretending a numerical score proves safety.
lessons.relationship: A test matrix crosses operating conditions with required behaviors
lessons.example: For a sensor board, test supply extremes, temperature range, cable attachment, reset during traffic, and sensor disconnection. Record the expected error report and recovery for each condition. An unexplained reboot is a failed diagnostic requirement even if the board later resumes output.
lessons.pitfall: One working prototype is not evidence of production yield, compliance, or long-term reliability.
lessons.exercise: Define a measurable requirement for sensor disconnection rather than saying the firmware should handle it gracefully.
lessons.solution: For example: detect disconnection within 100 ms, flag data invalid, report a specific fault, and resume only after a defined revalidation sequence. Choose timings appropriate to the application.

quiz.question: An LDO drops 5 V to 3 V at 0.1 A. Dissipation is:

modules.title: Edge intelligence and engineering capstones
modules.summary: Integrate disciplines and defend results with reproducible evidence.

lessons.title: Edge inference and resource budgets
lessons.explanation: An embedded ML model is one component of a sensing system. Data collection, preprocessing, memory, latency, energy, and failure behavior determine whether it is useful. Quantization represents values with fewer bits and introduces scale-dependent error. Evaluate the deployed arithmetic on representative held-out data, including unusual operating conditions. A smaller model is not automatically a better system if it loses the behavior the product needs.
lessons.relationship: Uniform affine quantization: q=clip(round(x/scale)+zero_point); reconstructed x=scale(q−zero_point)
lessons.example: With scale=0.1 and zero point=0, x=0.26 maps to q=3 and reconstructs as 0.3, an error of 0.04. Values outside the integer range saturate, creating a different error regime from small rounding noise.
lessons.pitfall: Accuracy measured on training data does not establish generalization, and a desktop timing result does not establish target-device latency.
lessons.exercise: Quantize x=−0.37 with scale=0.1 and zero point=0, assuming an adequate signed integer range.
lessons.solution: q=−4 and reconstructed x=−0.4; reconstruction error is −0.03 using reconstructed minus original.

lessons.title: Architecture tradeoffs and verification plans
lessons.explanation: A capstone should begin with requirements that can fail. Allocate timing, memory, power, and error budgets to subsystems, then identify the interfaces that carry assumptions between them. Compare alternatives using measured constraints rather than tool popularity. A verification plan connects each requirement to a test, retained artifact, and acceptance threshold. State which claims are simulation-only and which were demonstrated on hardware.
lessons.relationship: End-to-end latency includes acquisition + processing + queueing + communication + actuation
lessons.example: If acquisition takes 2 ms, processing 3 ms, queueing up to 4 ms, and actuation 1 ms, the budget is 10 ms. Ignoring queueing would understate the bound by 40%. Measurement must cover the same endpoints used by the requirement.
lessons.pitfall: A collection of individually passing modules can still fail at integration because their assumptions disagree.
lessons.exercise: Allocate a 20 ms latency requirement among four stages and describe how you would test the total.
lessons.solution: One possible allocation is 4, 6, 5, and 5 ms. Timestamp the defined input and output events under worst expected contention, and verify both stage and end-to-end limits.

lessons.title: Evidence, review, and portfolio delivery
lessons.explanation: An engineering portfolio should let another person reproduce a result and inspect its limits. Include the problem, architecture, interface contracts, implementation, tests, raw observations, and a discussion of failures. Separate a proposed feature from an implemented feature and a passing simulation from a measured board. Review is an opportunity to find incorrect assumptions before the artifact is reused. A polished demonstration is useful, but it does not replace the underlying evidence.
lessons.relationship: Requirement → test procedure → observed result → conclusion → known limitation
lessons.example: A sensor-to-decision capstone can retain a CSV trace, a latency histogram, a reproducible test command, and a fault-injection result. A CPU capstone can retain instruction traces, directed tests, and unsupported-instruction behavior. Each demonstrates a different claim and should be labeled accordingly.
lessons.pitfall: A screenshot of a waveform alone is insufficient for another learner to reproduce the experiment or diagnose a regression.
lessons.exercise: Write one defensible completion statement for a simulated robot controller and one claim you cannot make without hardware evidence.
lessons.solution: You can claim that specified simulated trajectories met their numerical error bounds. You cannot claim physical tracking accuracy, motor temperature, or real-world collision avoidance without corresponding validation.

quiz.question: A desktop simulation proves physical robot tracking accuracy.
quiz.explanation: Physical accuracy requires corresponding hardware validation.

projects.title: A trustworthy sensor node
projects.brief: Build a sampled sensor pipeline that quantizes, filters, frames, and validates measurements.
stages: Predict ADC codes and quantify clipping.
Implement an eight-sample moving average with an explicit startup policy.
Encode samples into bounded frames and reject malformed input.
Add an acquisition/processing latency budget and a sensor-disconnection state.
acceptance: Midscale input produces code 2048 in the stated 12-bit model.
Constant input settles to the same constant after eight samples.
Payload round-trips exactly; truncated and oversized frames are rejected.
Retain the sampling assumptions and a table of simulated versus measured claims.
projects.extension: Port acquisition to a microcontroller timer and DMA. Capture timestamps and dropped-sample counts on hardware. The Python model does not validate board timing.

projects.title: A robot that can explain its motion
projects.brief: Simulate differential-drive motion and compare integration with a closed-form constant-turn trajectory.
stages: Define body/world frames and units.
Integrate wheel velocities using an explicit time step.
Compare straight and circular trajectories with analytic predictions.
Add saturation, delayed sensing, and a stop-on-stale-command state.
acceptance: Equal wheel velocities produce zero heading change.
Opposite wheel velocities rotate the robot without translating in the ideal model.
Constant-turn position error is below 0.01 m at the supplied 1 ms time step.
Record how error changes when the step is halved.
projects.extension: Add obstacle inflation and a planner before considering a physical chassis. Physical collision avoidance and actuator limits require separate validation.

projects.title: A tiny processor you understand
projects.brief: Build an executable instruction model, then use it as a reference for a small RTL datapath.
stages: Specify register width, instruction semantics, and program termination.
Implement immediate load, add, and halt instructions.
Test wraparound, illegal instructions, and instruction limits.
Extend the model and implement the same contract in RTL.
acceptance: The demonstration adds 7 and 5 and halts with result 12.
Eight-bit addition wraps modulo 256.
Unsupported opcodes and missing termination raise explicit errors.
Do not call the teaching ISA a compliant RISC-V implementation.
projects.extension: Replace the teaching ISA with a documented RV32I subset, including decode and exception behavior. Add differential tests before expanding instruction coverage.

projects.title: A reproducible digital radio link
projects.brief: Simulate BPSK over Gaussian noise and compare measured bit errors with the analytic synchronized-channel model.
stages: State symbol energy and noise conventions.
Map seeded random bits to unit BPSK symbols.
Inject Gaussian noise, detect symbols, and count errors.
Sweep noise and add timing offset as a separate impairment.
acceptance: A noiseless channel returns all bits correctly.
At sigma=0.5, empirical BER is within 0.01 of the analytic value for 10000 seeded bits.
Store the random seed and sample count with results.
Explain why this model is not a complete RF modem.
projects.extension: Add pulse shaping, timing recovery, and a measured or simulated channel. Keep RF transmission as a separate equipment- and jurisdiction-dependent exercise.

projects.title: A well-specified SoC peripheral
projects.brief: Integrate a bounded FIFO with an address-decoded register interface and a testable reset contract.
stages: Write the address map and access permissions.
Implement data, occupancy, and reset registers.
Test full, empty, invalid address, and reset-with-data behavior.
Translate the contract to RTL with a specified bus handshake.
acceptance: Accepted writes emerge in FIFO order.
A full write returns failure without dropping old data.
Unaligned or unmapped accesses fail explicitly.
Reset clears occupancy and prevents stale valid reads.
projects.extension: Add a real APB or AXI-Lite wrapper, protocol assertions, CDC review, and synthesis constraints. The Python reference is transaction-level only.
